1: # Versioning Policy — SemVer Tag Governance
2: 
3: > [!CAUTION]
4: > **FLASH GATE — read this before every firmware upload.**
5: >
6: > Building for compilation testing is fine without tagging.
7: > But **before flashing to hardware**, if the firmware includes **any** new
8: > functionality since the last tag:
9: > 1. Check the current highest tag: `git describe --tags --abbrev=0`
10: > 2. Increment the dev PRE_NUM: `git tag v0.X.Y-dev.(N+1) && git push origin v0.X.Y-dev.(N+1)`
11: > 3. Rebuild (so `inject_version.py` picks up the new tag at compile time)
12: > 4. **Then** flash.
13: >
14: > This is **autonomous** — `dev` tags do not require user approval.
15: > Skip this step **only** if the firmware contains NO new functionality.
16: >
17: > **The sequence is: Tag → Build → Flash. Never flash an untagged build.**
18: 
19: ### Pre-flash checklist
20: 
21: Before calling `upload_firmware`, `agent_flash_monitor_verify`, or any
22: esptool/OTA upload command, stop and verify:
23: 
24: - [ ] Does this firmware contain new functionality since the last `dev` tag?
25: - [ ] If yes: have I tagged, pushed, **and rebuilt** so the version is baked in?
26: - [ ] `curl /api/system` after boot — does `firmware_version` match the new tag?
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ## Quick Reference
31: 
32: | Tag format              | Channel  | Agent can tag? | Requires user? |
33: |-------------------------|----------|---------------|----------------|
34: | `v0.X.Y-dev.N`         | Dev      | ✅ Yes         | No             |
35: | `v0.X.Y-beta.N`        | Beta     | ❌ No          | Yes            |
36: | `v0.X.Y`               | Stable   | ❌ No          | Yes            |
37: 
38: | Action                        | Agent autonomy | Requires user approval |
39: |-------------------------------|---------------|------------------------|
40: | Create `dev` tag              | ✅ Yes         | No                     |
41: | Create `beta` / `stable` tag  | ❌ No          | Yes                    |
42: | Increment `PATCH`/`MINOR`/`MAJOR` | ❌ No     | Yes                    |
43: | Run `deploy_release.py` (any) | ❌ No*          | Yes (User runs CLI)    |
44: 
45: * **Agents MUST NEVER execute `deploy_release.py` directly.** The private key requires an interactive passphrase, which causes background agent tasks to hang indefinitely on `openssl`. Always output the exact CLI command and ask the user to run it in their terminal.

Here is exactly how to set up the DHO804 for these captures:

### 1. Fix the 10X Probe Setting
1. Tap the **1 (CH1)** badge at the bottom left of the touch screen to open the channel menu.
2. In that menu, find the **Probe** setting and change it to **10X**.
3. Repeat the same for **CH2**.
*(Now it will read the true 3.3V instead of 330mV).*

### 2. Set Up the Screen
1. **Vertical:** Turn the vertical **SCALE** knobs for both CH1 and CH2 so they read **1 V/div** (you'll see this in the channel badges at the bottom). 
2. **Horizontal:** Turn the horizontal **SCALE** knob (top center) until the top of the screen says **10.0 ms/div**.

### 3. Take the First 3 Captures
If you plug a USB flash drive into the front of the scope, you can usually just press the **Quick Action** button (it often looks like a camera on Rigols) or use the save menu on the touch screen to grab a screenshot. Alternatively, clear photos from your phone are perfectly fine!

*   **Capture 1 (At rest):** Just take a photo/screenshot of the flat lines while you aren't touching the knob.

*   **Capture 2 (Knob UP):**

    2. Set **Source** to **CH1**, **Type** to Edge (Rising), and use the **LEVEL** knob to set the trigger line around **1.5V**.
    3. Press the physical **SINGLE** button in the trigger controls. The scope will say "Wait" or "Run".
    4. Turn the bike's resistance knob **UP**. The scope should catch the signal and freeze. Take your screenshot!

*   **Capture 3 (Knob DOWN):** 
    1. Press **SINGLE** again.
    2. Turn the resistance knob **DOWN**. *(Note: if the scope doesn't trigger, the signal might be coming down on CH2 instead of CH1. If so, just change the Trigger Source to CH2 and try again!)*

If you're asking about the **motor drive captures we're doing right now (Section C)**: No, we must measure voltage. 

Here's why:
1. **Safety:** You can never measure resistance on a circuit that has power running through it. Multimeters measure resistance by sending a tiny voltage of their own out through the probes. If the circuit is powered (like when the bike is trying to drive the motor), that incoming power fights the multimeter and will either give you completely random numbers or blow the fuse inside your multimeter. 
2. **What we're looking for:** We need to see the "shape" of the power the console is sending to the motor (whether it's a steady DC push or a pulsed PWM signal). The oscilloscope does exactly this by graphing voltage over time. Resistance wouldn't tell us how the motor is being driven.

Ah, I understand now! You want to see the resistance feedback (the potentiometer) changing *while* the motor is moving. That is a brilliant idea for visualizing how the closed-loop system works.

But even for the potentiometer, **you still need to measure voltage, not resistance**. Because the console is powered on, it is sending voltage through that potentiometer. The potentiometer acts as a voltage divider, outputting a variable voltage depending on the physical position of the motor.

Here is how you can set up your DHO804 to see exactly what you're looking for:

1.  **Keep CH1 on the Motor Drive:** Leave your CH1 probe on the **Red** wire (Motor +).
2.  **Move CH2 to the Potentiometer Wiper:** Move your CH2 probe to the **Blue** wire (this is the `POT_WIPER` signal). 
3.  *(Leave your scope ground clips on the Brown GND wire).*

The pot wiper (Blue wire) normally outputs a voltage between roughly **1.1V and 1.7V**, depending on the position of the motor. 

**To see them together:**
1. Set the trigger to **CH1** (so the scope catches the moment the motor starts driving).
2. Press **SINGLE**.
3. Turn the knob!

You should see CH1 jump up to 3.3V (the motor turning on), and at exactly the same time, you'll see CH2 (the Blue wire) start ramping up or down as the motor physically moves the potentiometer. When CH2 hits the target voltage, you'll see CH1 drop back to 0V (the motor turning off).

OK, I can see the data and there's a **big finding** here. There are two things happening:

### 1. No cadence events (type=0) — but that's expected right now
The cadence sensor connects to **GPIO 5**, and the GPIO ISR is set up on pin 5. However, the event log is dominated by **software threshold events**, not GPIO interrupts. Looking at the `handleSoftwareThresholds` code, channel 5 is actually being treated as a **motor channel** (not cadence) in the software threshold logic (line 256: `channel == 5 || channel == 6`). So those type=3/type=4 events on channel 5 are the ADC reading channel 5 (which is ADC1_CH5 = GPIO 6, the motor+ sense) crossing the motor threshold.

### 2. What IS being detected
- **type=3, channel=5** and **type=4, channel=6** — these are motor-onset/motor-off software threshold events. The ADC is reading something on channels 5 and 6 that's crossing the 500mV threshold. Since you haven't connected the motor dividers yet, this is likely just noise on floating pins.
- **type=2, channel=8** — these are Encoder Ch B threshold crossings, happening periodically (~18-21 seconds apart). Again, probably noise on a floating pin.

### The key issue
There's a **channel numbering mismatch** in the firmware. The ADC continuous driver uses ADC channel numbers (0-9), but the GPIO ISR uses GPIO pin numbers (5, 8). ADC1_CH5 on the ESP32-S3 is **not** GPIO 5 — it maps to a different physical pin. This is a bug we'll need to fix, but for now:

The ESP32-S3 features two SAR (Successive Approximation Register) ADCs. **ADC1** is typically preferred for analog sampling because, unlike ADC2, it is not restricted by the Wi-Fi driver[1].

### ESP32-S3 ADC1 Channel to GPIO Mapping
ADC1 on the ESP32-S3 consists of 10 channels, which are mapped to **GPIO1 through GPIO10**[1].

| ADC1 Channel | GPIO Pin |
| :--- | :--- |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_0 | GPIO1 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_1 | GPIO2 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_2 | GPIO3 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_3 | GPIO4 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_4 | GPIO5 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_5 | GPIO6 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_6 | GPIO7 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_7 | GPIO8 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_8 | GPIO9 |
| ADC1_CHANNEL_9 | GPIO10 |

### Important Considerations
*   **ADC2 Usage:** ADC2 (channels 0–9) is mapped to GPIO11–GPIO20[1]. However, keep in mind that **ADC2 cannot be used when Wi-Fi is active** because the Wi-Fi driver also utilizes this peripheral[1].

*   **Attenuation:** To measure voltages up to the full range (approx. 2.9V to 3.0V), ensure you configure the ADC attenuation to `ADC_ATTEN_DB_12`[2]. The default attenuation (0 dB) is typically limited to a much lower voltage range[3].
*   **Hardware Design:** If you are designing a custom PCB, refer to the official [ESP32-S3 Hardware Design Guidelines](https://www.espressif.com/en/support/download/documents) for the most accurate and up-to-date pinout information, as specific module variants (e.g., those with internal PSRAM) may have restrictions on certain pins[4][5].

## Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

### 1. Check Signal Levels and Range
*   **Voltage Saturation:** The ADC will return 4095 if the input voltage exceeds the maximum measurable range for the chosen attenuation[2][7]. Even though the ESP32-S3 can handle up to 3.3V, the linear range for the ADC is often lower depending on the `atten` setting[1][8].

*   **Floating Pins:** If the pin is not connected to a solid voltage source (e.g., a potentiometer or a voltage divider), it may pick up noise or "float" to a high voltage, resulting in a constant 4095 reading[10][7]. Ensure your signal source has a **common ground** with the ESP32-S3 board[7].

*   **One-Shot vs. Continuous Mode:** Ensure that your `adc_continuous` configuration is correctly initialized[4][11]. If your ESP32-S3 ADC is consistently reading **4095** (the maximum value for a 12-bit ADC), it indicates that the ADC is saturating at its upper limit[1][2]. This is rarely a driver bug and almost always a configuration or hardware issue[3][4].

Here are the most common causes and steps to resolve this:

### 1. Check for Floating Pins (Antenna Effect)
If the GPIO is not connected to a stable voltage source (e.g., a sensor or voltage divider), it will act as an antenna and pick up electromagnetic noise[5][6]. 
*   **Test:** Connect the GPIO directly to GND. The reading should drop to near 0. Then, connect it to 3.3V; the reading should be 4095. If it does not change, there is a configuration issue[7].
*   **Fix:** Ensure your sensor is providing a valid, low-impedance voltage. If you are testing, use a voltage divider (e.g., two 10kΩ resistors) to provide a known voltage (like 1.65V) to the pin[7].

### 2. Verify ADC Attenuation
The ESP32-S3 ADC has a limited linear range (typically ~1.1V by default)[1][2]. If you apply a voltage higher than the attenuation threshold, the ADC will saturate at 4095[2].
*   **Settings:**
    *   `ADC_ATTEN_DB_0`: ~950 mV range
    *   `ADC_ATTEN_DB_2_5`: ~1250 mV range
    *   `ADC_ATTEN_DB_6`: ~1750 mV range
    *   **`ADC_ATTEN_DB_12`**: ~2900–3100 mV range[1][2]
*   **Fix:** If you are measuring 3.3V, you **must** use `ADC_ATTEN_DB_12`[2]. Using lower attenuation with a 3.3V input will cause the reading to max out at 4095[2].

### 3. Check for Pin Conflict / IOMUX
The ESP32-S3 has a complex IOMUX[8]. Even if a pin is an ADC channel, it may be occupied by other functions (like I2C, SPI, or Flash/PSRAM)[9][10].
*   **Conflict:** Ensure GPIO 5 is not being initialized elsewhere in your code for another peripheral (e.g., as an output, I2C, or status LED)[9][4].

I'm estimating the RC settling time against the per-channel acquisition window and checking against the ESP32 TRM's recommended source impedance of under 10kΩ, since our 22kΩ exceeds that guideline.

That mismatch points to the 22kΩ source impedance preventing the sample-and-hold capacitor from discharging fast enough in the short acquisition window, so it stays locked near its previous high charge instead of tracking the real voltage drop — which looks like the actual root cause.

The Grey wire works fine since it idles near 0V and the capacitor has no high charge to discharge from, while the floating pins' noisy readings are consistent with partial, random settling. That suggests the fix is to lower the series resistance significantly, maybe down to 1kΩ or 4.7kΩ.

But at higher rates the acquisition window per sample could be just a few microseconds, which might actually be the real bottleneck rather than the sample rate itself. "## Phase 2: Findings Summary

### Root Causes

| # | Bug | Location | Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | `GPIO_PULLUP_ENABLE` on GPIO 5 and 8 | SignalLogger.cpp:138 | GPIO 5 pegged HIGH through 22kΩ. Cadence reed switch signal can't pull it low enough. Violates hardware spec §5.5 no-pulls rule. |
| **2** | Floating unconnected pins generating spurious threshold events | SignalLogger.cpp:256-274 | Event ring buffer saturated with 4000 garbage events from floating GPIO 6/7. Real cadence events (if any) are lost. |
| **3** | Dashboard shows nothing because the `/api/echenon/live` endpoint reports raw ADC values, not interpreted signals | EchenonModule.cpp:111-142 | No user-friendly cadence RPM, just raw ADC channel numbers 0-9. |

### Why You Can't See Cadence

1. The internal pull-up on GPIO 5 holds the pin at 3.3V (ADC reads 4095).
2. The cadence reed switch needs to pull GPIO 5 to GND through the 22kΩ
   series resistor. But the internal pull-up (~45kΩ) creates a voltage
   divider: 45k/(45k+22k) × 3.3V ≈ 2.2V. That's not a clean LOW — the
   reed switch closure would only pull the pin down to ~2.2V instead of 0V.
3. The GPIO ISR is set to `ANYEDGE`, so it might still fire, but the
   transition may not be clean enough to register reliably.
4. Even if cadence events ARE generated, the ring buffer is already full of
   4000 garbage motor-threshold events from the floating GPIO 6/7 pins.

### Recommended Fix

Change line 138 in `SignalLogger.cpp`:
```cpp
// BEFORE (violates hardware spec §5.5)
io_conf.pull_up_en = GPIO_PULLUP_ENABLE;

// AFTER
io_conf.pull_up_en = GPIO_PULLUP_DISABLE;
```

And suppress software threshold processing for unconnected channels until they
are wired up, or add a guard that skips threshold events when the raw ADC
value is clearly floating (wide min/max spread with no stable baseline)."

args.ReplacementContent:
"### 5.5 Direct-Tap Series Resistors (RS1–RS8) and the No-Pulls Rule

The eight direct taps (every tap except GPIO 6/7) each have a **4.7 kΩ series
resistor**, placed at the harness end of the tail.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Bench-tested 2026-10-03:** The original 22 kΩ value exceeded the ESP32-S3
> ADC continuous-mode source-impedance limit (Espressif recommends < 10 kΩ).
> At 83 kHz aggregate sample rate the S/H capacitor could not settle through
> 22 kΩ during brief reed-switch closures (~50 ms). Replaced with 4.7 kΩ +
> 100 nF ceramic cap on the ESP32 side. Cadence detection confirmed at
> 74–120 RPM.

**Why — back-powering.** Each ESP32 pad has ESD clamp diodes to its 3.3V
supply. If the ESP32 is unpowered (USB unplugged, or during boot/brown-out)
while the console is on, the console's 3.3V lines — pot reference (Yellow),
wiper (Blue), encoder VCC and channels, cadence — would drive current
through those diodes into the ESP32's rail and try to power it. That loads
the pot reference and the encoder supply, which are exactly what register
rows 4, 6, 8 and 10 measure, and can disturb the console. 4.7 kΩ limits any
such current to about 0.7 mA, which is still low enough to avoid measurably
loading the console's lines.

**No pulls.** Every tap pin is configured with **no internal pull-up or
pull-down**. An internal pull (~45 kΩ) on a cadence or encoder pin would bias
the console's own line and change what is being measured.

**Decoupling capacitor (C1).** A 100 nF ceramic capacitor is placed between
each ADC signal pin and GND on the ESP32 side of the series resistor. This
provides a low-impedance charge reservoir for the ADC's sample-and-hold
capacitor, ensuring accurate readings even with the 4.7 kΩ source impedance."
args.TargetContent:
"### 5.5 Direct-Tap Series Resistors (RS1–RS8) and the No-Pulls Rule

The eight direct taps (every tap except GPIO 6/7) each have a **22 kΩ series
resistor** (10–47 kΩ acceptable), placed at the harness end of the tail.

**Why — back-powering.** Each ESP32 pad has ESD clamp diodes to its 3.3V
supply. If the ESP32 is unpowered (USB unplugged, or during boot/brown-out)
while the console is on, the console's 3.3V lines — pot reference (Yellow),
wiper (Blue), encoder VCC and channels, cadence — would drive current
through those diodes into the ESP32's rail and try to power it. That loads
the pot reference and the encoder supply, which are exactly what register
rows 4, 6, 8 and 10 measure, and can disturb the console. 22 kΩ limits any
such current to about 0.1 mA, so the console's lines are not measurably
loaded.

**No pulls.** Every tap pin is configured with **no internal pull-up or
pull-down**. An internal pull (~45 kΩ) on a cadence or encoder pin would bias
the console's own line and change what is being measured.

**Side effects to check (WO0 spike):** the series resistance slows ADC
sampling-capacitor settling at kHz sample rates and adds a small RC to
digital edges. The WO0 spike confirms ADC-continuous accuracy through 22 kΩ
and whether one pad can be ADC-sampled while serving a GPIO interrupt
(GPIO 5, 8, 9). If C2 is fitted, it goes on the ESP32 side of RS1 so it
never loads the console's wiper line."

416: ### 5.4 Motor Sense Voltage Dividers (R1a/R1b, R2a/R2b)
417: 
418: The motor is driven bidirectionally by the console's H-bridge — Red goes HIGH
419: while Black goes LOW (forward), then the reverse for backward. Back-EMF when
420: the motor stops can also push wires below ground.
421: 
422: The 30kΩ + 10kΩ divider is **protection and scaling only**, not a
423: logic-level interface:
424: 
425: ```
426: Motor wire ──► R1a/R2a (30kΩ) ──┬──► GPIO (reads divided voltage, ADC1)
427:                                 │
428:                             R1b/R2b (10kΩ)
429:                                 │
430:                                GND
431: 
432: Division ratio: 10k / (30k + 10k) = 1/4   → pin stays ≤ 3.3V up to ~13V drive
433: ```
434: 
435: | Motor wire voltage | GPIO sees | Current through divider | Safe? |
436: |---|---|---|---|
437: | 3.3V (DC drive) | 0.825V | 0.08 mA | ⚠️ At V_IL max. Read as analog. |
438: | 0V (idle) | 0V | 0 mA | ✅ Clean LOW |

"# B01 — Sensor Bring-Up Report (Phase 0)

**Date:** 2026-10-03  
**Board:** EX-3 on Waveshare ESP32-S3-Nano  
**Firmware:** `v0.1.0-dev.4` on branch `fix/adc-gpio-conflict`  
**Operator:** mcneillm  
**IP:** 192.168.20.187 (WiFi: cb-iot)

---

## 1. Executive Summary

Incremental sensor bring-up session connecting the bike console's loom
to the ESP32 one signal group at a time. Three of four signal groups
confirmed working. One critical root cause discovered and resolved:
the original 22 kΩ series resistors exceed the ESP32-S3 ADC continuous-mode
source-impedance limit, preventing detection of brief transient signals
(cadence reed switch).

## 2. Firmware Bugs Found & Fixed

| # | Bug | Root Cause | Fix | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `GPIO_PULLUP_ENABLE` on GPIO 5/8 | Violated hardware spec §5.5 no-pulls rule. Internal pull-up created voltage divider with 22 kΩ series resistor. | Changed to `GPIO_PULLUP_DISABLE` | `v0.1.0-dev.2` |
| 2 | `gpio_config(GPIO_MODE_INPUT)` called after `adc_continuous_start()` | Disconnected GPIO 5/8 from ADC analog peripheral, reconnected to digital GPIO matrix. | Removed `gpio_config`, `gpio_input_enable`, and GPIO ISR handler entirely. Cadence now uses ADC software thresholds (type=0 events). | `v0.1.0-dev.3` |
| 3 | `adc_digi_pattern_config_t` array not zero-initialised | Potential garbage in padding bytes. | Changed to `adc_pattern[10] = {}` | `v0.1.0-dev.4` |

## 3. Hardware Root Cause — ADC Source Impedance

### Problem

The ESP32-S3 ADC continuous (DMA) driver samples at 83,333 Hz aggregate
across 10 channels. Each channel's sample-and-hold (S/H) capacitor has a
very short acquisition window (~1–2 µs). Espressif recommends **< 10 kΩ
source impedance** for the ADC.

The original 22 kΩ series resistors (hardware spec §5.5) created an RC time
constant too long for the S/H to settle during brief signal transients. For
the cadence reed switch (~20–50 ms closure at 50–120 RPM), the S/H capacitor
could not discharge from 3.

5: It supports multiple quadrature encoders simultaneously — up to

**The problem:** The EncoderModule uses the **ESP-IDF PCNT (Pulse Counter) peripheral**, which needs **digital GPIO inputs**. But our encoder signals are currently being sampled by the **ADC continuous driver** on GPIO 8/9. These two peripherals can't share the same pins simultaneously — we hit exactly this conflict earlier with the `gpio_config` bug.

**Two approaches to analyse the encoder:**

1. **ADC burst capture (diagnostic — no code changes):** Use the existing burst buffer to capture 1-5 seconds of raw analog data at ~8kHz per channel while you turn the knob. This gives us the actual waveforms — we can see bounce, noise, transition times, and whether the encoder is generating clean quadrature. Best for **diagnosing the hardware quality**.

2. **Add EncoderModule (functional — needs code changes):** Remove CH7/CH8 from the ADC scan pattern, add `WITH_ENCODER` to the build, wire up a `BoardEncoder` descriptor pointing at GPIO 8/9, and register the module. This gives us debounced position counting with acceleration. Best for **getting a smooth reading**.

I'd suggest we do **approach 1 first** — burst-capture the raw encoder signals to understand the hardware quality. Then if the signals look clean enough, we add the EncoderModule for a proper reading. If they're noisy/bouncy, we'll know the console's flakiness is the encoder itself, not the software.

Great forward-thinking. A few thoughts:

**256 levels** is the right choice — `uint8_t`, clean binary, and gives you ~0.06 mm displacement resolution per step. Easy to map both ways:

```
echelon_level = internal_level * 32 / 256    // or >> 3
peloton_level = internal_level * 100 / 256
```

**The goalseek problem is the critical design risk.** The Echelon console's control loop is:

```
1. Encoder click → console computes target pot position
2. Drive motor until pot == target (bang-bang, with overshoot)
3. Stop
```

If we MITM the encoder and command a position that's, say, halfway between two "natural" Echelon levels, the console will drive the motor to a pot position it doesn't recognise as a valid stop point. Three possible outcomes:

| Scenario | What happens | Likelihood |
|---|---|---|
| **Console converges anyway** | It targets the nearest valid pot window and stops | Likely if it uses a tolerance band |
| **Console hunts forever** | Motor oscillates between two positions, never settling | Possible if tolerance is tight |
| **Console snaps to nearest level** | It rounds to the closest known level and displays that | Most likely |

The motor seek data supports scenario 3 — the console already uses a ±15 ADC count tolerance band (~40% of a level step), and the bang-bang controller always overshoots and corrects. It's clearly targeting discrete pot windows, not exact values.

**The real question is: do we even need to send encoder signals to the console at all?** If we're doing full MITM, we could:

- **Option A:** Intercept encoder, translate, forward modified quadrature to console — console stays in control of the motor. Risk: goalseek divergence.
- **Option B:** Intercept encoder AND motor drive. ESP32 directly commands the motor via its own PID loop, using the pot for feedback. Console is bypassed entirely for resistance control. Clean but complex — need H-bridge control.
- **Option C:** Let the console handle motor control normally, but use the pot reading to detect the current level and report it in our own coordinate system. Encoder passes through unmodified. No MITM risk, just monitoring + remapping.

These are architectural decisions for a later phase. Want me to capture these options in the analysis doc, or is this more of a design spec discussion for when we get to the MITM work order?

"# MITM Encoder — Design Notes

**Status:** Early thinking — not yet a work order  
**Date:** 2026-10-04  
**Context:** Findings from encoder & resistance analysis (see `encoder-resistance-analysis.md`)

---

## 1. Core Requirement

The Echelon app must remain functional and continue to report resistance
level, calories, power output, etc. This means the Echelon console must
continue to receive encoder signals and control the motor. We cannot
bypass the console — we must work *through* it.

## 2. Internal Resolution

Use **256 internal levels** (`uint8_t`) as the canonical resistance scale.
External mappings:

```
echelon_level  = internal_level * 32 / 256     // Echelon 1-32
peloton_level  = internal_level * 100 / 256    // Peloton 1-100
internal_level = echelon_level * 256 / 32      // reverse
```

256 gives ~0.06 mm displacement resolution per step on the eccentric cam.

## 3. Architecture: Intercept, Translate, Forward

```
Physical Encoder
       │
       ▼
 ┌─────────────┐
 │  ESP32 PCNT  │  ← hardware debounce, acceleration
 │  (ingest)    │
 └──────┬──────┘
        │
        ▼
 ┌─────────────┐
 │  Translation │  ← 256-level internal model
 │  & Remap     │     linearisation, acceleration curves
 └──────┬──────┘
        │
        ▼
 ┌─────────────┐
 │  Quadrature  │  ← synthesise clean A/B signals
 │  Output GPIO │     to Echelon console encoder input
 └──────┬──────┘
        │
        ▼
 Echelon Console
 (motor control, app reporting, calories, power)
```

The ESP32 sits between the physical encoder and the console's encoder
input. It ingests the noisy signal via PCNT, translates it through the
internal 256-level model, and outputs a clean synthesised quadrature
signal that the console's decoder can reliably read.

## 10. Architecture Spectrum

There are four levels of MITM integration, ranging from passive
monitoring to full simulation. The decision depends on how much control
we need vs. hardware complexity.

```
 Passive ◄────────────────────────────────────► Full Control
   Tap        Encoder MITM     Full MITM      Console Bypass

| Level | Encoder | Pot | Motor | What it gives us |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Monitor** | Tap | Tap | Console | Read-only telemetry |
| **Encoder MITM** | Intercept + resynth | Tap | Console | Clean input, console stays in control |
| **Full MITM** | Intercept + resynth | **Simulate** | Console | Tell console any level we want |
| **Console bypass** | Intercept | Read | **ESP32 H-bridge** | Total control, console is display-only |

### Pot Simulation Considerations

If we simulate the pot, we can decouple the reported level from the
physical motor position. This enables:
- Reporting arbitrary levels to the Echelon app
- ERG mode (external app sets target, ESP32 drives to it)
- Non-standard resistance curves (e.g., truly linear, exponential)

**Hardware options for pot simulation:**
- **DAC output** (e.g., MCP4725) — simplest, I²C, 12-bit
- **Digital potentiometer** (e.g., MCP4131) — drop-in replacement for
  the physical pot, SPI, maintains the console's expected impedance
- **PWM + RC filter** — cheapest, but resolution and ripple may be issues

**Risk:** If we simulate the pot, the console's motor control loop will
try to goalseek to the position we're reporting. If the physical motor
position doesn't match the simulated pot value, the motor will run
continuously trying to reach an unreachable target. We would need to
either:
1. Also control the motor (full bypass), or
2. Always keep the simulated pot value tracking the actual motor position,
   only deviating transiently to "nudge" the console

1: # EncoderModule
2: 
3: `EncoderModule` (`modules/EncoderModule/EncoderModule.hpp`) is a pure-service
4: rotary encoder manager built on the ESP-IDF PCNT (pulse counter) peripheral.
5: It supports multiple quadrature encoders simultaneously — up to
6: `MAX_ENCODERS` (`SOC_PCNT_UNITS_PER_GROUP` on real hardware, 4 on native
7: builds), one PCNT unit per encoder.
8: 
9: Implements [`ITickable`](../../interfaces/tickable.md) and
10: [`IMCPContributor`](../../interfaces/mcp-contributor.md).
11: 
12: ## Enablement
13: 
14: Gated by the `WITH_ENCODER` build flag. Not compiled in unless this flag is
15: defined in `platformio.ini`.
16: 
17: ## Descriptor Types (`include/EncoderConfig.h`)
18: 
19: - **`BoardEncoder`**: `id`, `pinA`/`pinB` (quadrature GPIOs), `stepsPerDetent`
20:   (raw PCNT counts per physical detent, typically 2 or 4), `reversed`
21:   (flip CW/CCW), `accel` (`EncoderAccelConfig`).
22: - **`EncoderAccelConfig`**: `enabled`, `deadZoneMs`, `shortCutoffMs`,
23:   `maxMultiplier` — velocity-based acceleration curve parameters.
24: - **`EncoderDelta`** enum: `RAW`, `ACCELERATED` — consumption mode for
25:   `consumeDelta()`/`consumeDeltaAt()`.
26: - **`EncoderEvent`**: EventBus payload — `id`, `delta` (normalised detent
27:   steps), `velocityMs` (inter-pulse interval).
28: 
29: Per-board encoder descriptors are declared in `hardware/<board>/board.h` as a
30: `BOARD_ENCODERS[]` array, gated by `WITH_ENCODER`.
31: 
32: ## Registration Pattern
33: 
34: `addEncoder()` must be called for every descr
<truncated 201 bytes>
 adds the module to the framework's tick list. Mirror
38: `sample-app/src/main.cpp`:
39: 
40: ```cpp
41: for (size_t i = 0; i < BOARD_ENCODER_COUNT; i++) {
42:     encoderModule.addEncoder(BOARD_ENCODERS[i]);
43: }
44: encoderModule.begin(app);
45: app.registerModule(&encoderModule);
46: ```
47: 
48: ## Dual Consumption Model
49: 
50: `tick()` reads all PCNT counters, normalises to detent steps, computes
51: velocity-based acceleration, and updates per-encoder atomic accumulators —
52: consumers can use either or both models concurrently:
53: 
54: 1. **Push (EventBus)** — publishes topic `encoder.rotate`, payload
55:    `EncoderEvent*`, once per encoder per tick when movement occurred. See
56:    [systems/event-bus/framework-topics.md](../event-bus/framework-topics.md)
57:    ("Module-Published Topics" — only present when `WITH_ENCODER` is compiled
58:    in).
59: 2. **Pull (atomic accumulators)** — `consumeDelta(mode)` (first/only encoder,
60:    convenience wrapper) and `consumeDeltaAt(index, mode)` atomically extract
61:    and reset the accumulated detent count for a given `EncoderDelta` mode
62:    (`RAW` unscaled, `ACCELERATED` velocity-scaled). Thread-safe; intended for
63:    consumers that poll on their own cadence rather than subscribing to the
64:    bus — e.g. an LVGL input driver's read callback.
65:

68: `adapters/lvgl/CrowPanel128Adapter` consumes `EncoderModule` via the pull API:
69: its `lv_indev_t` encoder read callback calls

71: focus-group navigation.
